title: Title and occasion: Mossgiel, November 1785
short: Written at Mossgiel farm, Ayrshire, after Burns's plough broke open a field-mouse's winter nest; printed in the Kilmarnock Poems of 1786.
body: The full title fixes the poem to a working moment: 'on turning her up in her nest with the plough, November, 1785'. Burns's brother Gilbert, who farmed Mossgiel with him, later reported that the poem was composed while Robert was still holding the plough. A further tradition, told by early editors on the recollection of the farm-hand John Blane, says that the boy chased the mouse to kill it and was called back by his master. Whether or not the poem was literally made in the furrow, the anecdote shaped its reception as the work of a 'ploughman poet'. It appeared in Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect (Kilmarnock, 1786), the volume that made Burns famous. The address to a small creature, mixing comic diminutives with serious moral reflection, belongs with 'To a Louse' and 'To a Mountain Daisy' in the same book.

title: sleekit
short: Sleek, smooth-coated; the Kilmarnock-based glosses give simply 'sleek'.
body: The adjective describes the mouse's glossy fur, and the line's run of diminutive epithets ('wee', 'cow'rin', 'tim'rous', 'beastie') establishes a tone of affectionate pity. Modern Scots speakers often hear 'sleekit' in its extended sense of 'sly, smooth-mannered, untrustworthy', and some readers enjoy the hint that the speaker half expects the mouse to be a thief (as stanza 3 admits). But the primary sense here is physical, as editors gloss it; the poem's movement is towards sympathy, not suspicion. Note the elisions marked by apostrophes ('cow'rin', 'tim'rous'): they record spoken Ayrshire pronunciation and keep the four-stress line quick.

title: The 'Standard Habbie' (Burns stanza)
short: Six lines rhyming aaabab: three tetrameters, a short dimeter, a tetrameter, and a closing dimeter that often lands a punchline.
body: Burns writes in the stanza named 'Standard Habbie' after Robert Sempill of Beltrees's mock-elegy on the Kilbarchan piper Habbie Simson (c. 1640); Allan Ramsay gave it the name, and Ramsay and Robert Fergusson made it the chief vehicle of eighteenth-century Scots vernacular verse before Burns used it so often that it is also called the 'Burns stanza'. The short fourth and sixth lines act like a bob or tag: here 'Wi' bickering brattle!' and 'Wi' murd'ring pattle!' Its usual associations are comic and satirical, so Burns's use of it for compassion and, at the end, near-despair is part of the poem's surprise. The rhyme scheme in RPO's description is aaabab.

title: bickering brattle
short: A hurrying, clattering scamper; RPO glosses the phrase 'hurrying scamper'.
body: 'Brattle' in Scots is a clattering noise or a short, sudden rush; the Scottish National Dictionary also records the verb 'to move quickly with a clatter of feet'. 'Bickering' (Kilmarnock 'bickerin') is the Scots verb 'bicker', to move quickly with a pattering sound, used of running water and of quick feet. Together the alliterating words make a comically loud noise for so small an animal, seen from the mouse's panic. The line is the stanza's first short 'tag' line.

title: pattle
short: The plough-staff: a small spade-like tool carried on the plough to clear earth from the blade.
body: The pattle (or pettle) was a short staff with a flat blade, used to scrape clay and soil off the mould-board or ploughshare. The Scottish National Dictionary cites this very line under the word. 'Murd'ring' turns a farm tool into a weapon, and the speaker refuses to use it. The detail fits the farm-hand tradition that the boy ran after the mouse to kill it and was stopped. The hyperbole is half comic, but it prepares for the poem's serious account of human power over creatures.

title: man's dominion
short: Recalls God's grant to humankind of 'dominion' over every creature in Genesis 1, here regretted for breaking nature's fellowship.
body: In Genesis 1:26-28 God gives man 'dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing'. Burns, raised on Scripture in Calvinist Ayrshire, takes the word but tilts it: dominion has become domination, and it has 'broken' a prior 'social union'. The apology ('I'm truly sorry') is mock-formal and also sincere. Critics commonly read the stanza against eighteenth-century ideas of sympathy and of a lost harmony between creatures, ideas that Burns knew from Pope and the moral philosophers.

title: nature's social union
short: An Enlightenment idea: all creatures were once bound in natural fellowship, which human mastery has broken.
body: The phrase sounds like moral philosophy rather than farm talk, and the shift into polished English diction is deliberate. Pope's Essay on Man (1733-34), Epistle III, imagines an original 'state of Nature' in which 'Man walk'd with beast, joint tenant of the shade', a harmony later destroyed by human tyranny over animals; Burns knew Pope well. The idea also chimes with the Scottish Enlightenment's stress on sympathy and fellow-feeling. The 'ill opinion' of the next line is the mouse's justified fear of man. Critics note how Burns makes the abstract phrase concrete by setting it beside a ruined nest.

title: earth-born companion / fellow-mortal
short: Man and mouse are both made of earth and both must die: Genesis 2:7 and 3:19 lie behind the phrase.
body: In Genesis man is formed 'of the dust of the ground' (2:7) and told 'dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return' (3:19). Burns uses this shared origin to level the hierarchy that 'dominion' set up: the ploughman and the mouse are companions in being 'earth-born' and 'fellow-mortal'. 'Fellow-mortal' is the stanza's climactic tag-line, and its seriousness is unusual for the stanza form. The idea anticipates the last stanzas, where the comparison will turn against the man.

title: thou may thieve ... thou maun live
short: The speaker concedes that the mouse steals grain, and excuses it: 'What then? ... thou maun [must] live!'
body: 'Whiles' means 'sometimes' and 'maun' means 'must'. The mouse is a pest, and the farmer knows it; the stanza's generosity lies in his calculation that its theft is trivial against the need to live. The colloquial shrug 'What then?' keeps the tone conversational. Readers have compared the argument with the moral sense that need excuses small theft, but Burns's emphasis is practical and neighbourly rather than legal.

title: A daimen icker in a thrave
short: An occasional ear of corn out of a thrave (twenty-four sheaves): a tiny share of the harvest.
body: 'Daimen' means rare, occasional; the Scottish National Dictionary quotes this line under the phrase 'daimen-icker'. An 'icker' is a single ear of grain. A 'thrave' was a measure of cut corn, reckoned at twenty-four sheaves (two stooks of twelve). The farmer's arithmetic shows how little the mouse takes. The gesture also recalls the biblical law that the harvester should leave the gleanings and the corners of his field 'for the poor and stranger' (Leviticus 19:9-10), which is perhaps why he expects 'a blessin' for it.

title: the lave
short: 'The lave' is 'the rest, the remainder': the farmer will be blessed in the rest of his crop.
body: The Scots noun 'lave' (Old English laf, 'remainder') is common in Burns; RPO glosses it 'rest'. The line half-seriously claims that sparing the mouse's portion will bring God's blessing on what remains, a proverbial piety that gives the generosity a comic edge. 'An' never miss't!' closes the stanza with a shrug.  The idiom is that of farm proverb: a little given away is a blessing on the whole.

title: silly wa's
short: 'Silly' means frail, feeble, flimsy; the walls ('wa's') of the nest are being scattered by the wind.
body: The older English and Scots sense of 'silly' is 'helpless, deserving pity, weak' (compare 'silly sheep'), not 'foolish'; RPO glosses it 'feeble'. 'Wa's' is 'walls' and 'win's' is 'winds'. The comic diminutive 'wee bit housie' and the domestic word 'walls' turn the nest into a little cottage, so that its ruin anticipates the human theme of eviction in stanza 6. Many of Burns's tenant-farming neighbours knew that fear.

title: big ... foggage green
short: 'Big' is 'build'; 'foggage' is coarse grass or aftergrass, the material the mouse would need for a new nest.
body: The Scottish National Dictionary defines foggage as regrowth of grass after haymaking, or rough grass left uneaten among the stubble, and quotes these lines. RPO glosses 'big' as 'build' and 'foggage' as 'coarse grass'. In November there is nothing green to build with, so the loss is final. The stanza moves from the ruin itself to the season, with December's winds in the tag-lines.

title: snell
short: Sharp, biting, piercing (of wind or cold); RPO glosses 'piercing'.
body: 'Snell' is an old word shared by Scots and northern English (Old English snell, 'quick, active'), which in Scots came to mean bitterly cold and cutting, of weather. Paired with the English 'keen', it doubles the sense, a common Burns habit of setting a Scots word beside its English equivalent. The tag line ends the stanza on the threat of winter, which the next stanza dramatises.

title: coulter / cell
short: The coulter is the vertical iron blade fixed in front of the ploughshare to cut the turf; 'cell' is the mouse's chamber.
body: The coulter (Latin culter, 'knife') slices the soil before the share turns it. 'Cruel' gives the tool the guilt its user feels. The dash and the exclamation 'Till crash!' break the stanza's syntax as the blade breaks the nest. 'Cell' suggests a hermit's or monk's small room, and so gives the mouse a kind of dignity; the word also anticipates 'house or hald' in the next stanza.

title: But house or hald
short: 'Without house or holding': the mouse is now homeless.
body: 'But' here is the Scots preposition 'without'. 'Hald' is 'hold', a holding or place of shelter; RPO glosses the phrase 'house or habitation' and compares 'Address to the Deil'. The alliterating legal-sounding pair suits a tenancy: the mouse is evicted from the home it laboured over, a fate many Scottish tenant farmers feared in the 1780s, including Burns's own family at Lochlea and Mossgiel.

title: thole
short: To endure, to bear patiently: from Old English þolian.
body: The Scottish National Dictionary cites this very line under the sense 'to suffer, endure'. The word was once general English (Old English þolian, Old Norse þola) but survived chiefly in Scots and northern dialects. The mouse must endure the 'sleety dribble' (the sleet dripping through) and the frost of the following tag-line. Burns uses it again in 'The Twa Dogs' of tenants who must 'thole a factor's snash' (put up with a land-agent's abuse), a reminder that the mouse's endurance mirrors that of poor farmers.

title: cranreuch
short: Hoar-frost; 'cauld' is 'cold'.
body: The Scottish National Dictionary defines 'cranreuch' as hoar-frost and treats it as a Scots word of probably Gaelic origin, the second part perhaps reòthadh, 'frost'. It closes the stanza with a strong, rough-sounding Scots word, typical of how Burns saves his densest dialect for physical hardship.

title: no thy lane
short: 'Not alone': the mouse is not the only creature whose foresight proves vain.
body: The Scots idiom 'my lane', 'thy lane' means 'by myself, by yourself, alone'; RPO glosses 'no thy lane' as 'not alone'. The phrase opens the turn of the poem from the mouse to the human condition. The mouse 'proved' (tested and found) that foresight may be useless; so do men. The construction is idiomatic in Scots ('his lane', 'their lane') and has no exact English equivalent. Here it introduces a fellowship of failure between the speaker and the mouse, the closest the two come in the poem.

title: The best-laid schemes ... Gang aft agley
short: The poem's most famous lines, now proverbial: careful plans of mice and men often go wrong.
body: 'Gang aft' is 'go often'. The lines generalise the mouse's loss into a statement about all planning, and their currency as a proverb is largely Burns's doing; John Steinbeck took the title Of Mice and Men (1937) from them. The archive's text prints 'o' mice an 'men' with a misplaced apostrophe; the Kilmarnock text reads 'o' Mice an' Men'. In context the lines are not consoling: they lead to 'grief an' pain' instead of 'promis'd joy'. Biographers relate the gloom to Burns's own position in 1785-86, with the Mossgiel farm failing and plans to emigrate to Jamaica.

title: agley
short: Askew, awry, wrong: from Scots 'gley', to squint.
body: The Scottish National Dictionary explains 'agley' as 'a-' plus 'gley', a squint, so that the literal sense is 'squinting, askew' or 'off target', and the figurative 'wrong, awry'. Its earliest dated quotation is this line from 'To a Mouse'. RPO glosses it 'amiss'. The image is of an aim that goes astray, a plan that misses its mark. Because the lines became proverbial, they are often quoted in anglicised form ('go oft awry'), which loses the Scots word's visual image of a squint.

title: The present only toucheth thee
short: The final reversal: the mouse is luckier than the man, since it lives only in the present, while he remembers the past and fears the future.
body: The diction moves into formal English ('toucheth', 'prospects drear') for the moral, then back to Scots in 'Och!' and 'canna'. The thought, that animals are spared knowledge of the future, has a long history; Pope's Essay on Man, Epistle I, says that Heaven 'from all creatures hides the book of Fate' and that the lamb, if it had human reason, could not play as it does. Burns turns the commonplace personal: the man looks back on 'prospects drear' and forward with guessing fear. Biographers connect the mood with Burns's troubles of 1785-86. The ending reverses the poem's starting hierarchy, in which the man pitied the frightened beast.
